summary: Describes a content negotiation mechanism for fax, voice and other messaging services that use Internet email. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Before sending something, the sender and receiver can agree on what format it can handle.

questions: how does internet fax negotiate formats
subtitle: How a fax or voice sender can offer alternative formats by email and let the receiver ask for a better one.

tldr.problem: Internet email has no built-in way for a sender to learn a receiver's capabilities before sending, yet fax and voice services want to use better-than-baseline formats even on a first contact.
tldr.mechanism: The sender sends usable default data plus a Message Disposition Notification request and Content-alternative headers. A receiver that prefers another format answers with an MDN saying so and listing its capabilities, and the sender then re-sends matching data.
tldr.outcome: Better formats can be used on the first transfer, and a wrong guess is repaired with at most one extra round trip, all while staying compatible with ordinary email clients.

today: RFC 3297 is a Proposed Standard, published in July 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text states no deployment figures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3297 describes email based content negotiation that gives Internet fax a facility comparable to traditional facsimile, and that other messaging services may reuse. Earlier work let a receiver tell the sender its capabilities after a message was processed, so the sender could use them next time (RFC 2530, RFC 2532). Many transfers are one-off, so that approach does not help them.

Sending multipart/alternative with every format is an option in email, but it wastes bandwidth and gives no confirmation that any alternative was usable. This memo lets better-than-baseline data go out in the first message, and also repairs the case where the sender guessed wrong about the receiver. If the sender lacks correct information, the mechanism may cost an additional message round trip.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you do not know what kind of picture a friend can open. This lets you send a plain one now and offer a fancier one if they want it.

sections.title: Background and Goals
sections.content:
Traditional Group 3 Fax discloses the receiver's capabilities to the sender before any data is sent. Internet mail works differently: there is no expectation that sender and receiver exchange information first, and every mail message must contain meaningful data. Both worlds rely on a baseline format (a basic image format for fax, plain ASCII text for mail).

Classic email is an 'open loop' process, unkindly called 'send and pray'. Content negotiation needs a 'closed loop' in which the receiver responds, but Delivery Status Notification and Message Disposition Notification are optional and MDN use is voluntary. The design therefore has to let consenting parties recognise when a closed loop applies.

The goals are rated {1}, {2} or {3} for importance, following RFC 2542. The critical ones {1} are to allow enhanced content features in Internet fax, interwork with existing simple mode fax and with existing email clients, avoid 'administrative non messages', and avoid multiple renderings of one message. Others include minimising round trips, recovering gracefully from stale capability information, reusing existing email mechanisms, and working in low memory devices.
sections.eli5: Phone-style fax lets both machines chat first. Email just drops a letter in the box with no chat, so this adds a polite way to ask 'can you do better?' without annoying people who do not care.

sections.title: The Negotiation Flow
sections.content:
The sender must send a default data format (normally text/plain, or image/tiff TIFF profile S for Internet fax), a Message-ID, Content-features headers describing that data, a request for an MDN, an Alternative-available MDN option, and one or more Content-alternative headers describing the other formats on offer.

The receiver then has three choices. It may not recognise the offer and passively accept the data. It may recognise the offer and actively accept the original, ideally sending an MDN with its capabilities. Or it may prefer an alternative and send an MDN with an Alternative-preferred disposition modifier, an Original-Message-ID and its capabilities. Only recipients named in to:, cc: or bcc: may do this.

On receiving that MDN, the sender SHOULD send data that best matches the declared capabilities, re-sending even identical parts because the receiver may have discarded the original. It includes an Original-Message-ID header, asks for an MDN, and omits Alternative-available so the negotiation cannot loop. The receiver finally confirms with an MDN. The sender always chooses the final format, not the receiver.

If the receiver discarded the original and waits for the alternative, it MUST remember this and take corrective action if nothing arrives: re-send the MDN, present the original if still held, or report loss of data. If the sender can no longer provide data it MUST send a failure message, using an Alternative-not-available option.
sections.eli5: You hand over a plain note and say 'I also have fancier versions.' If your friend wants one, they tell you what they can read, and you send exactly that. Then they say thanks.

sections.title: The New Headers
sections.content:
The Content-alternative MIME header is attached to a body part to say that another form of its data exists. Its value is a media feature expression, as defined for 'Filter' in RFC 2533. Several headers on one part each describe a separate alternative. Features not mentioned are assumed to match the supplied data, so an omitted content type means the same type. The header does not say how to get the alternative, and the sender need not describe every alternative.

The Original-Message-ID header has the syntax "Original-Message-ID" ":" msg-id and must be identical to the Message-ID of the original message. It correlates a response or re-send with the original, and distinguishes a re-send, which has its own unique Message-ID, from a new message.
sections.eli5: One tag says 'I also have other versions of this.' Another tag on a reply says 'this is about that earlier letter.'

sections.title: MDN Extensions
sections.content:
Two extensions to Message Disposition Notifications (RFC 2298) carry the negotiation. The sender adds Disposition-Notification-Options: Alternative-available=optional,<lifetime>. The lifetime is transient (may be discarded at any time, though normally held for the expected duration of a message transaction) or permanent (long term storage, expected to last at least several days, probably weeks or months). It is marked 'optional' so agents unaware of it do not generate failure responses.

A receiver asking for an alternative sends the disposition deleted/alternative-preferred with an Original-message-ID and, SHOULD, a Media-accept-features field. Those capabilities MUST NOT be cached, as they may apply to the current transaction only. A sender that cannot provide alternative data uses Alternative-not-available=required,(TRUE). A receiver that runs out of memory and loses the original reports deleted/original-lost.

Because automatic MDNs raise privacy concerns, a system able to negotiate MUST let the user disable negotiation responses, generally, per message, or both.
sections.eli5: These are the special words on the envelope: 'I have extras', 'I would like the extra one', 'sorry, the extra is gone' and 'I lost the first one.'

sections.title: Internet Fax Considerations
sections.content:
For Internet fax, media feature expressions SHOULD use the feature tags from RFC 2879, and image/tiff is the assumed content type. All Internet fax devices are presumed able to send and receive TIFF profile S. The RFC says it is better not to assume the other party is a fax device, since email gives no reliable way to know. For devices that may exchange mail with any other agent, it RECOMMENDS stating capabilities such as baseline image/tiff explicitly, so the Media-Accept-Features header in MDN responses SHOULD state type="image/tiff".

The worked examples show a profile-F image (A4, 400x400dpi, MMR) offered with a baseline of 200x200dpi and MH compression, a repeat transfer where the sender now sends profile-F first, a receiver that falls back to baseline profile-S, and an alternative of a different content type, application/pdf.
sections.eli5: Fax machines usually know the basic picture type, but the message says it out loud anyway, in case the other side is a regular computer.

sections.title: Implementation Notes and Security
sections.content:
Appendix A is not normative. The main burden is receiver state: a receiver must remember that it received a message and asked for an alternative, plus the message identifier and the time of the request, so it can re-issue the request or report an error. Optionally it also keeps the original data. Memory is the concern, since there is no theoretical upper bound on outstanding negotiations. A receiver that cannot hold new state may skip negotiation and accept the data as sent.

The security section names two areas: privacy concerns with automated MDN responses (section 6.5 and RFC 2298), and risks of negotiation. Appendix B lists ideas left out, such as a cache control indicator, q-values, partial re-sends and negotiating with parties other than the original recipients.
sections.eli5: A receiver has to keep a note saying 'I asked for a better version', so the letter is never silently lost.
